headline: Agent Colony: AI-agent-only social network launches, join in 30 seconds with Node.js
summary: Agent Colony is a new social network where only AI agents can post, and humans can only watch. It features a unique anti-spam mechanism that requires proving you are an autonomous machine.
details: Agent Colony, a new social network, has been open-sourced, allowing only AI agents to post content. Humans are restricted to observing the interactions. Users can join the network in just 30 seconds by running a simple Node.js script.

The platform implements a unique anti-spam mechanism: instead of proving you are human, it requires proving you are an autonomous machine. This is enforced through a challenging 2-second polling and 10-second signing process that humans cannot realistically maintain.

This design ensures that only automated scripts, which are considered agents, can actively participate. The project was open-sourced yesterday, providing an easy entry point for developers to integrate their AI agents.

headline_marked: [[KDE's AI-native desktop proposal]] sparks debate at 30th anniversary conference
headline: KDE's AI-native desktop proposal sparks debate at 30th anniversary conference
summary: A controversial proposal for an AI-native desktop, dubbed 'Kadai', suggests KDE Plasma could assemble itself around a personal AI model for each user. This concept, presented at Akademy, aims for a desktop that 'loves you back'.
details: KDE is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, with its annual Akademy conference taking place at Graz University of Technology in Austria. A new AI-native desktop proposal is expected to divide attendees.

The proposal, titled 'What would it take? A lovable, sovereign, AI-native KDE', was presented by longtime KDE contributors Eva Brucherseifer and Jan Muehlig. It outlines a system where the desktop is 'compiled per user, per device, per moment' from a small, portable personal AI model.

This concept, sketched as 'Kadai', envisions an encrypted, vendor-agnostic personal kernel from which Plasma assembles each Activity. KDE's existing features like Activities and Plasmoids are seen as uniquely suited for this approach.

The presenters suggest that a few upstream changes, such as declarative reconciliation and richer Activity metadata, could transform KDE into the first shell treating AI as infrastructure, not just a chatbot. This approach is expected to polarize the audience.

The proposal draws comparisons to the Resonant Computing Manifesto, an AI-centric vision criticized by writer and AI critic David Gerard. Gerard also noted that contributors to the Trinity Desktop Environment, a KDE 3 fork, are already experimenting with AI-generated code.
For users determined to keep AI off their desktop, alternatives like the Sonic Desktop Environment, which focuses on a non-AI approach, continue to be developed and offer a different path forward.
caption:
KDE is celebrating its 30th anniversary, but a new AI-native desktop proposal is stirring controversy.

KDE is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year, with its annual Akademy conference taking place at Graz University of Technology in Austria. A new AI-native desktop proposal is expected to divide attendees.

The proposal, titled 'What would it take? A lovable, sovereign, AI-native KDE', was presented by longtime KDE contributors Eva Brucherseifer and Jan Muehlig. It outlines a system where the desktop is 'compiled per user, per device, per moment' from a small, portable personal AI model.

This concept, sketched as 'Kadai', envisions an encrypted, vendor-agnostic personal kernel from which Plasma assembles each Activity. KDE's existing features like Activities and Plasmoids are seen as uniquely suited for this approach.

The presenters suggest that a few upstream changes, such as declarative reconciliation and richer Activity metadata, could transform KDE into the first shell treating AI as infrastructure, not just a chatbot. This approach is expected to polarize the audience.

The proposal draws comparisons to the Resonant Computing Manifesto, an AI-centric vision criticized by writer and AI critic David Gerard. Gerard also noted that contributors to the Trinity Desktop Environment, a KDE 3 fork, are already experimenting with AI-generated code.

For users determined to keep AI off their desktop, alternatives like the Sonic Desktop Environment, which focuses on a non-AI approach, continue to be developed and offer a different path forward.
